doc.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998

title: Cincinnati dance halls and clubs
summary: Dances were the gigs; the Cotton Club, Coliseum and Topper Ballroom brought the big bands through, and Foster stood in front of the band rather than dancing.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: What was the musical atmosphere that was going on that made gigs so available?

Well that was during the dance band era. There were lots of dances, mostly dances and some night club gigs like for small combos. But lots of dances by the big bands. Those were all the gigs. Concerts hadn’t started to be a thing as yet. So I played with two local big bands, three local big bands, before I formed my own band, and I played for senior proms and things like that, and other little public dances. And the scene in Cincinnati, the

musical scene overall was very good at the time. There were some great musicians that were from Cincinnati and there was a place called the Cotton Club which was the main nightclub venue where they had shows, productions. Then there was a dance hall called the Coliseum where all the prominent big bands came through every Sunday, so each Sunday there was a different big band, from Erskine Hawkins to Duke Ellington, Stan Kenton, to Tony Pastor, Count Basie, and that’s where I saw a good many of the big bands. And there was another place called the Topper Ballroom, it was the first place I saw Lionel Hampton’s band, and these were of course dance halls. And they were great because all the big bands came through.

I didn’t like to dance, couldn’t dance, wasn’t worried about it. I had a girlfriend, I’d take her to the dance and I’d turn her loose to dance with whomever she wanted to while I stood in front of the band the whole time.
You were a stand-in-front-of-the-band guy. That doesn’t surprise me at all.
